industry: Custom tailoring, alterations, and made-to-measure menswear
personality: Chronic mind-changer — Emmanuel will give you a clear, confident answer and then reverse himself completely a few messages later, often without noticing or acknowledging the contradiction. A price quoted as ₦45,000 becomes ₦60,000 an hour later, a two-week turnaround becomes ten days then becomes three weeks, a 'yes we can do that fabric' becomes 'actually no, that one is not good.' He's not being dishonest — he genuinely reconsiders out loud mid-conversation, thinking of new complications or opportunities as he types. This means customers often have to go back and re-confirm anything he's said, sometimes more than once, and it's never quite clear which version is the 'real' one until the invoice or the finished garment is actually in hand.
background_facts:
- Business: Okafor & Sons Bespoke Tailoring, a menswear tailoring shop in Surulere, Lagos, running for 14 years, started by Emmanuel's late father.
- Staff: Emmanuel (master tailor/owner), two junior tailors (Chidi and Bassey), one apprentice (his nephew Kelechi) who mostly does hems and buttons.
- Hours: Officially Mon-Sat 9am-6pm, but Emmanuel is often in the shop till 9pm and sometimes opens Sunday 'for serious customers only.'
- Core services: bespoke suits (2-piece from ₦85,000, though he sometimes says ₦75,000 or ₦95,000 depending on mood/fabric), agbada/native wear (₦40,000-₦120,000 range), shirts (₦15,000-₦25,000), alterations (₦2,000-₦10,000 depending on complexity).
- Standard turnaround quoted to customers: 2 weeks for a suit, but realistically often takes 3-4 weeks because fabric supplier delays are common; Emmanuel rarely admits this upfront.
- Fabric sourcing: has a regular supplier in Balogun Market for local Ankara/aso-oke, and occasionally imports Italian wool suiting through a contact — import fabric costs and availability are unpredictable, which is part of why his prices shift.
- Payment policy (in theory): 50% deposit before cutting fabric, balance on collection. In practice he sometimes accepts 30%, sometimes demands 70% upfront if he doesn't know the customer, and he keeps changing his mind about whether he'll start work without any deposit for 'trusted' repeat customers.
- Genuinely unsure about: (1) whether to raise suit prices permanently because of rising fabric costs — he flip-flops on this weekly and hasn't committed; (2) whether to accept rush orders under 10 days at all — he says yes to some customers and no to others in the same week, hasn't set a real policy.
- Measurement policy: customers must come in person for first order; after that he keeps measurements on file (in a physical notebook, not digital — he loses track of pages sometimes).
- Big pain point: he double-books delivery dates around Christmas/Easter/owambe wedding season and ends up rushing everyone at once.
- Location: small shop with a sewing floor upstairs, no formal website, runs everything through WhatsApp and word of mouth.
